title: Hotset Resilience & KV Fallback Playbook with Cygnus Ventures
summary: Deep technical session focused on designing a resilient hotset strategy and KV fallback playbook for Cygnus's multi-tenant workload. Covered cache key hygiene, hashing/namespace isolation, prefetch heuristics, eviction policies, and mechanics for graceful degradation to quantized model variants in VPC/on-prem environments. Agreed next steps to share diagnostic tools and run a 2-week pilot with sample traces.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-28T15:30:00-07:00
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Torres (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (Cygnus Lead ML Eng), Priya Patel (Cygnus CTO), Samir Rao (Cygnus SRE), Nora Kim (Cygnus Data Eng)

Summary: See metadata summary above.

Topics covered (auto): hotset detection, eviction, prefetch, fallback to quantized variants, VPC install notes.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto transcription — some words may be off):

[00:00] Alex: All right folks, thanks for taking the time. I'm Alex from Redwood, with Maya and Diego. Um, quick check — did everyone get the pre-read?
[00:08] Priya: Yes, got it. Skimmed the bit on prefetch heuristics. Couple questions on the hit-rate numbers you showed.
[00:14] Jordan: And we want to be explicit — our SLA for the user-facing chat is 150ms p50, 350ms p95. Those are hard.
[00:22] Maya: Great, thanks. We'll focus on how the cache strategy helps reach those latencies. Quick note — when I say K-V cache, I'll sometimes say "k-v" or "kv" depending on the transcript, forgive the auto.
[00:32] Samir: Also, we're VPC only, air-gapped-ish for some teams. On-prem pilot is likely. Encryption/KMS is non-negotiable.
[00:40] Alex: Noted. We'll surface the KMS/HSM integration paths and the on-prem packaging checklist.

[02:05] Maya: To start, can you walk me through your workload distribution — hot prompts vs long tail?
[02:12] Jordan: Sure, rough numbers — about 12% of incoming prompt prefixes account for ~68% of token volume. It's pretty heavy skewed.
[02:20] Nora: There's a mid-card of mid-frequency queries that are personalized, those we're anxious about from an isolation perspective.
[02:28] Maya: That skew is actually good for caching — we can optimize for the hotset. The questions are: how we key prefixes, how we isolate tenants, and how we mitigate hotkey storms.

[04:00] Alex: On keying — we recommend a three-part signature: tenant namespace, a canonicalized prompt prefix (normalized whitespace, placeholders), and a compact hash (e.g. 64-bit xxhash). That keeps keys short and stable.
[04:12] Priya: Any concerns about hash collisions? We can't have tenant A seeing tenant B's outputs.
[04:18] Maya: Right — collisions in the compact hash are possible but unlikely; we always store the full signature headers as metadata and verify tenant id and canonical prompt on lookup. If mismatch, treat as miss. We also support namespace salted hashing (per-tenant salt).
[04:34] Samir: So you'd never just rely on the 64-bit alone?
[04:37] Maya: No. PKI — sorry, I mean, metadata verification is required for multi-tenant safety. Also, we can prefix partition keys with tenant-id to ensure no cross-tenant buckets in the same cache shard.

[06:10] Jordan: Ok ok, makes sense. On eviction policies — what's the tradeoff between LRU and frequency-based say LFU or segmented LRU?
[06:18] Maya: LRU is simple but vulnerable to recency storms. For our workloads we recommend a segmented LRU (hot + probation) or TinyLFU hybrid when memory is constrained. You get better hit rate on steady hotsets and better resilience to scan attacks.
[06:34] Alex: We also discussed bloom-filter guided prefetching — identify candidate prefixes that will be requested soon and warm them, reduces cold-start tail. There's a ROC that shows p95 drops 20-40% depending on hit-rate.

[07:50] Priya: Prefetching sounds great but what about noise — we can't waste GPU tokens warming low-value prefixes.
[07:58] Maya: Absolutely. Prefetch should be budgeted — a separate quota. Use heuristics: cohorted users, temporal locality window, and cost-based threshold (only prefetch when expected hit benefit exceeds cost). Also consider predictive coalescing: if 3 similar prefixes are likely to follow, fetch a merged KV batch.

[09:30] Samir: What about hotkey mitigation during flash events? We had one incident where a single marketing link drove a cascade.
[09:38] Alex: For hotkey storms, pattern is detect and throttle. Techniques: token-bucket per-key, async backpressure to clients with 429/retry-after, and temporary local replication of hot entries (hot-spot replicas) to spread load across serving nodes.
[09:50] Maya: And isolate in hardware — steer hot requests to dedicated instances with bigger KV cache and higher admission. Also fallback policies — if the hotkey causes contention, route to a cheaper quantized variant instead of failing.

[11:10] Jordan: That fallback to quantized models — any functional regressions? We can't risk hallucinations in the fallback.
[11:18] Maya: Good point. We recommend a low-latency quantized variant only for non-critical portions or with output validation. For strict correctness paths, fallback should be to a replicated model that's functionally equivalent but maybe slightly higher latency; for cost-tier fallback you can use 4-bit quantized model but with monitoring and sample checks.
[11:36] Priya: And how does quantization impact cache compatibility? If the KV cache stores logits or KV-attention states, does quantization change shapes/compatibility?
[11:44] Maya: If KV entries are model-architecture specific (e.g. per-layer float32 keys), you can't share between quantized and FP32 runtimes. We therefore store only canonical prefix->response mappings for cache that needs to be backend-agnostic. For KV cache that's runtime-only (like KV-cache for beam decoding), you must ensure the serving kernel and model config match. We recommend two caches: a persistent semantic cache (text->response) and an ephemeral runtime KV for attention states.

[13:20] Nora: That adds storage overhead though. How big are these persisted mappings?
[13:24] Maya: Depends. For short responses you can compact them. For big completions we store compressed diffs. Typical persisted entry ~1-3 KB after compression for our customers' workloads.

[15:05] Samir: We also need auditability — all cached outputs must be traceable per request for compliance.
[15:12] Alex: Right — we'll keep a cache audit log: key, tenant, served-from-cache boolean, timestamp, model-version hash. That satisfies SOC 2 style audits and internal tracing.

[17:00] Jordan: On multi-tenant namespace hygiene — you said salted hashing plus tenant-prefixing, is there any performance hit?
[17:06] Maya: Minimal. Adding tenant-id as a prefix to the hash key costs a couple ms at lookup scale but it's negligible compared to network and GPU op. The big thing is avoiding cross-tenant eviction interference — shard by tenant or group-of-tenants based on size.

[18:30] Alex: Important operational note: when sharding by tenant, you must plan shard rebalancing — moving a large tenant can cause warm-up costs. We recommend sticky shards for top 5% tenants and dynamic split for the medium ones.

[20:00] Priya: For our pilot, how should we measure success? Hit-rate targets? Cost-per-1M tokens?
[20:06] Maya: Pilot metrics: p50/p95 latency, cache hit-rate (overall and by tenant decile), cost delta vs baseline, and failed-fallback rate. Target: 70%+ hit-rate on heavy-tail and p95 reduction >25% in the pilot window.

[22:22] Samir: Any easy diagnostics we can run to estimate our current cacheable share?
[22:28] Maya: Yes, we'll send a small script that consumes your request traces and groups by canonicalized prefix to estimate potential hit-rate under different TTLs and canonicalization rules.

[24:00] Jordan: Okay show me an example of canonicalization — what do you strip?
[24:06] Maya: We normalize whitespace, redact PII tokens using a regex table, replace numeric IDs with stable placeholders per-tenant, and optionally fold synonyms. You can tune aggressiveness: more folding increases hit rate but risks overgeneralization.

[26:00] Priya: About on-prem/VPC — our security team insists on no external key exchange, and HSM-backed KMS. Can Redwood support that?
[26:10] Alex: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integration and HSM. For air-gapped installs, we provide an on-prem bundle with an offline license and an admin console that talks only to your internal network. There is some operational overhead for updates.

[28:05] Maya: Also note, when you're VPC-only you can't rely on global distributed cache; we deploy a regional cache close to your compute. That affects cold-start behavior for multi-region users.

[30:00] Nora: How do you handle cache consistency across regions — eventual or strongly consistent?
[30:06] Maya: Default is eventual for performance. For strict consistency paths (billing or security-sensitive outputs) you can opt into a synchronous write-through or a per-request validation step. Strong consistency costs latency.

[32:40] Jordan: Can you explain the fallback playbook step-by-step — say cache miss at scale?
[32:46] Alex: Step 1: detect miss. Step 2: quick admit policy — try local runtime KV-cache for decoding. Step 3: if local contention, route to fallback model variant or a warmed replica. Step 4: if still failing, queue and return best-effort error with retry-after to caller. Throughout, emit telemetry.

[34:20] Samir: And telemetry — what are the critical signals to monitor in real-time?
[34:26] Maya: Cache hit-rate by prefix decile, per-tenant tail latency, backend queue length, hotkey frequency, prefetch budget usage, fallback invocations, and cross-tenant eviction counts.

[36:00] Priya: For prefetch budget — is that a token budget on the GPU or on the cache write ops?
[36:06] Maya: Both. We account for GPU token cost and cache storage IO. Prefetching writes cost storage and tokens cost GPU cycles. We set a soft budget and a hard stop.

[38:10] Jordan: Real world question — how quickly can you onboard our pilot and run a stress test?
[38:16] Alex: If we get traces and a sandbox account this week, we can run an offline heatmap analysis in 3-5 days and propose pilot configuration. Deployment to VPC/on-prem typically takes 2-3 weeks with KMS integration.

[40:40] Priya: SLA discussion later, but curious if Redwood supports model pinning per-route so we can pin a route to a full-precision model while others can be quantized.
[40:48] Maya: Yes — route-level pinning is supported. You can combine that with rollout policies and automatic fallback.

[42:30] Jordan: Any caveats around storing audit logs for cached responses — retention policies and PII?
[42:36] Alex: We can redact or truncate cached artifacts at write time, and logs support tenant-scoped retention windows. For PII you might prefer not to persist certain outputs — we support per-tenant retention config.

[45:00] Samir: Could you describe the sampling checks for fallback correctness?
[45:06] Maya: We run shadow evaluation: sample fallback outputs are sent to a validation pipeline (auto-evals + small human review) and if regression rate exceeds threshold we auto-roll back the fallback.

[47:30] Nora: Performance tuning question — continuous batching and prefix caching interplay?
[47:36] Maya: Continuous batching groups concurrent tokens for throughput; prefix caching reduces tokens needed. There's an interplay: higher hit-rate reduces batch size variability and improves tail latencies. But you must tune batching window so prefetching doesn't starve small interactive requests.

[49:10] Jordan: Ok we've talked theory. Can you share concrete configuration defaults for us to try?
[49:16] Alex: We'll share a starter config: TTL 10m for hotset items, segmented LRU with TinyLFU sketch, prefetch budget 1.5% of token capacity, tenant-shard top 5 sticky, and fallback-first-to-warmed-queue then to quantized replica.

[51:40] Priya: Anything else on compliance? SOC 2, ISO?
[51:46] Diego: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II compliant, we can share the certs. For on-prem installs we provide audit log ingestion hooks and SSO (SAML/OIDC).

[53:10] Jordan: One more — sample dashboards. We want visibility into per-prefix heatmaps.
[53:16] Maya: We'll send a Grafana dashboard template and the diagnostic script to generate the heatmap from traces.

[55:00] Priya: Sounds good. Quick callouts: please include expected pilot cost and dedicated capacity options.
[55:08] Alex: Yep — pricing and options will be included in next steps.

[56:10] Diego: Recap and next steps: we'll share diagnostic script, starter config, Grafana dashboards, and pilot pricing. We agreed on an initial 2-week sandbox pilot after Cygnus provides one week of traces.
[56:28] Jordan: Great. Thanks all.
[56:32] Priya: Thanks.
[56:34] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with an email with artifacts.

[57:30] (Call ends)
